notes.title: How does shade change a street?
notes.body:
FIELD OBSERVATION · Riverside walk

The shaded side of the street stayed noticeably busier during our afternoon walk. People stopped near the trees, while the exposed benches were mostly empty.

Questions to follow
• Is shade the main reason, or does seating matter just as much?
• What changes between midday and the evening commute?
• How could we record dwell time without collecting personal data?

Next visit
Return at 12:00 and 17:30. Sketch the shade boundary and count occupied seats in ten-minute intervals. Compare a weekday with a weekend.

Working assumption
A comfortable place to pause may matter as much as a quicker route. This is a hypothesis to investigate, not a conclusion.

Synthetic example — no real participants or measured findings.

notes.title: 把访谈中的停顿也记下来
notes.body:
方法备忘

访谈不只记录受访者说了什么，也留意他们何时停下来思考。

下一步：在试访谈中用时间戳记录停顿，再核对录音，避免把观察误写成解释。

虚构示例，不包含真实参与者资料。

notes.title: A small question about public seating
notes.body:
Would a movable chair change how people use the courtyard?

Look for examples with both individual seating and shared tables.

Synthetic research prompt.

notes.title: Comparing neighborhood cooling strategies across different street widths, tree coverage, building heights and everyday patterns of use
notes.body:
LITERATURE REVIEW · Working outline

Compare shade, surface materials, ventilation and access to drinking water. Separate measured outcomes from design recommendations.

Evidence to collect
1. Study location, climate and season.
2. Measurement method and observation window.
3. Who benefits, at which times of day?
4. Maintenance needs and possible trade-offs.

Do not compare temperature readings without checking the instrument height, exposure and time.

Follow-up questions
How are nighttime conditions reported? Does the study account for accessible routes and places to rest? What information would a neighborhood team need before making a small reversible trial?
